title: From Wishes to Action: What Cognitive Science Can Teach Us About Teacher Motivation and CPD
author: Haili Hughes
summary: Haili Hughes uses a cognitive science paper on how people represent goals, Chandra, Saxe, Ragan-Kelley and Tenenbaum's work on a language of thought, to explain why some teachers engage deeply with CPD while others only attend. Her argument is that motivation depends on imagining a valuable, achievable future classroom state, so broad topics like questioning are weak motivators compared with specific outcomes. She draws on the paper's wants versus wishes distinction to say good CPD converts vague wishes into actionable goals. She adds that goals are socially embedded, so aligning individual aims with collective purpose and pupil outcomes raises engagement, and that goals tied to professional identity create commitment rather than compliance. She closes with a four-question goal-setting model for CPD and a challenge to leaders to help teachers turn wishes into actions.
points: CPD motivates when it links to a concrete, imagined future classroom outcome rather than a broad theme such as questioning or literacy.
A want can guide action while a wish may not, so effective CPD helps teachers convert vague aspirations into specific, time-bound goals.
Teacher motivation is social: aligning personal goals with pupils' success and shared school purpose makes CPD feel relevant.
Goals tied to who a teacher wants to become produce commitment, while imposed targets produce compliance.
A four-question cycle (desired outcome, why it matters, next action, how to tell it works) turns motivation into action and reflection.
quotes: A vague wish such as “I want to get better at behaviour management” may express a genuine desire, but it does not necessarily guide action.
Over the next four weeks, I will establish and practise a consistent entry routine with Year 8, then review whether it reduces disruption at the start of lessons.

Many teachers have wishes for their practice: they wish pupils were more engaged, wish marking felt more manageable, wish they felt more confident with a new specification. CPD becomes motivational when it helps transform those wishes into actionable goals.
This helps explain why CPD is more powerful when it aligns individual teacher goals with collective purpose.
A good coaching conversation might begin with: “What do you want pupils to be doing differently by the end of this half-term?” This question encourages the teacher to imagine a concrete future state.
A target imposed from outside may create compliance, but a goal connected to professional identity can create commitment.
The challenge for school leaders is not simply to provide CPD, but to help teachers turn professional wishes into actionable goals.
